body.heading: Words that refuse to pick a direction
paragraphs: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Racecar is the classic: spell it from the back and you still get racecar. Level, civic, radar, kayak and refer all do the same trick, quietly hiding in everyday English.
Numbers can join in too. 121, 1331 and 12321 are palindromes, and the date 02/02/2020 read the same both ways in several date formats, which made it a small celebration for word lovers.

body.heading: From words to whole sentences
paragraphs: With spaces and punctuation ignored, whole sentences can fold back on themselves. The most famous is “A man, a plan, a canal: Panama”, written about the building of the Panama Canal. Another favourite is “Was it a car or a cat I saw?”

The longest single-word palindrome in the Oxford English Dictionary is often said to be tattarrattat, a made-up word for a knock on the door coined by James Joyce in his novel Ulysses. It runs to twelve letters, all arranged around a centre that never changes.

body.heading: Try it: build your own
paragraphs: Start small. Take a short word, write its reverse next to it, and see how close you are: if the two match, you have found one. Then try names — Anna, Hannah, Otto and Eve are palindromes already, which is why they appear in so many puzzles.

For a bigger challenge, try to write a sentence that works both ways. Pick a short pivot word for the middle, build matching pairs of words around it, and be patient. It is fiddly, satisfying, and a lovely way to feel how letters balance.

takeaway: A palindrome is a small act of symmetry: build one yourself and you will start spotting them everywhere.
